items.finding: Both regions update the seat inventory counter, and last-write-wins resolves the conflict, so the same seat can be sold in both regions: Scenario 1 in 3.3 ends with two buyers for seat A-12 while the counter reads 0. That breaks the zero-tolerance double-booking rule; the counter needs one writer, a conditional reservation or a merge rule.

The recovery targets do not match the service targets or the data: the design's RPO of 60 seconds (3.2, 6.3) is twice the 30-second RPO service-targets.md sets for transactional data, and the measured P99 replication lag (420-720 ms, max 2.2 s) is 4-7 times the design's own < 100 ms P99 lag target and success criterion 4.

A DNS TTL of 300 seconds (3.5, dns-config.json) means clients keep resolving the failed region for up to 5 minutes after Route 53 changes, so failover cannot meet the 60-second RTO; the 6.2 breakdown counts only 20 seconds for DNS propagation.

The cost analysis (3.9, with no figures in 8.1) prices 1 TB of database storage once although each of the two RDS instances needs it, leaves out the Multi-AZ standbys, and its one-time total ($48,000; $47,400 in budget-breakdown.yaml) already exceeds the $45,000 approved budget.

The failback steps (3.7, 7.1) say only 'verify replication has caught up'; they give no check or pass criterion and no step to reconcile writes the surviving region accepted while the other was down, so returning traffic can reintroduce conflicting seat and payment rows.

The design states three different recovery times: RTO 120 seconds in 3.2, an estimated 90 seconds in 3.6 and a 60-second RTO in 6.2, so there is no single target to build or test against; only 60 seconds matches service-targets.md.
Asynchronous replication with eventual consistency for seat counts (3.2, 3.3) contradicts the strong consistency service-targets.md requires for ticket inventory and for payment records.
